subject: Cloud Computing
title: Stateless vs. Stateful Services
description: A 60-second lesson on Stateless vs. Stateful Services.

hook.text: A stateless server treats every request like a stranger. It remembers nothing between calls.

buildup.text: Stateless services store no session data locally. Any server can handle any request — perfect for scaling.

discovery.text: State gets stored externally: in databases, caches, or session stores. The service itself stays clean and disposable.

twist.text: Stateful services — like databases and game servers — are much harder to scale. They can't be easily replaced.

climax.text: Cloud-native design pushes state to the edges: managed databases and caches. Everything else stays stateless.

punchline.text: Stateless scales easily. Stateful is where the hard problems live.

quiz.question: Why are stateless services easier to scale in the cloud?
options: Any server can handle any request since no session data is stored locally
Stateless services use less memory than stateful ones
Cloud providers only charge for stateless services

details.summary: Stateless services store no client data between requests, making them easy to scale and replace. Stateful services maintain data across requests, requiring sticky sessions or external state stores. Most cloud patterns favor stateless services with externalized state.
details.whyItMatters: Statelessness is the key enabler of horizontal scaling and auto-scaling. Understanding when and how to externalize state is fundamental to cloud-native design.
takeaways: Stateless services can be freely replicated and replaced
State is externalized to databases, caches, or object stores
Auto-scaling works best with stateless service instances

faq.question: Where should externalized state be stored?
faq.answer: Redis or Memcached for session data and caches, relational or NoSQL databases for persistent data, and object storage for files and blobs. The choice depends on access patterns, durability requirements, and latency needs.

faq.question: Are databases stateful services?
faq.answer: Yes. Databases are inherently stateful because they persist data. Cloud-managed databases handle the complexity of stateful operation, including replication, failover, and backup, so application developers can focus on stateless application tiers.
